newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines move on property loans should reassure.
newsitem.headline: Philippines move on property loans should reassure.

text.p: Economists were divided over the benefits of the Philippines' Central Bank move on Tuesday to limit banks' loan exposure to the real estate sector, but said it should provide some reassurance to nervous investors.
Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson announced that the Monetary Board had ordered banks to limit their loans to property developers and homeowners to 20 percent of their total loan portfolios.
It also lowered the loan value to 60 percent from the previous 70 percent of a property's appraised value.
Banks have one year to comply with the 20 percent limit.

Though the quality of banking loans has not been proven to be deteriorating, the measures would calm concerns over the possibility of a repeat of the Thailand banking crisis, caused by a glut of property projects and falling asset prices.

"It is very obvious that people are worried about it. This is a good way to reassure the people, especially the armchair analysts," Johnny Noe Ravalo, chief economist of the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), told Reuters.
The Philippine stock market fell on Tuesday to its lowest level in two years on fears the property sector, facing a glut of projects, could pull banks down with it.
The index fell 128.87 points, or 4.54 percent, to 2,708.44.
Singson said the two measures are "designed to prevent banks from overlending to the real estate sector that could undermine the country's financial system".
"This is a positive development," said one banking analyst who recently recommended a sell in the banking industry.
"At least, the Central Bank is acknowledging this concern," he said, adding the measures would not impact the revenue stream of large-sized banks which carry more diverse portfolios.
Mid-sized banks and mortgage banks would have a more difficult time to comply.
A leading economist from a domestic commercial bank said the measures were unnecessary since individual banks had their own internal risk management controls.
"Any policy that will curtail banking lending activity is counterproductive," he said.
He also dismissed parallels between Manila and Thailand's property woes as overblown.
The Central Bank said exposure to the real estate sector was at 10.9 percent of the total outstanding loans, with a past due ratio of only 1.15 percent.
It added that 70.3 percent of the loans were fully secured, while the remaining amount was extended to high net-worth individuals and companies with good credit ratings.
"So, are we fighting our own shadows? Perhaps the answer is yes. But the ghost has been created and it has caused a panic scare in the market," Ravalo said.
